# The Lobbyist of Small Hours

There's a man who sits at the diner on Fifth and Clement every night between 2:00 and 4:00 AM. I don't know his name. I've never asked. He drinks black coffee and eats eggs over easy and writes in a leather journal with a fountain pen that he uncaps with a ceremony that suggests the act of writing is still, to him, sacred.

I've watched him do this perhaps forty times now.

Here's what I think about when I see him: he might be the most important person in the city, and none of us know it. He might be writing the email that saves six hundred jobs. He might be drafting a letter that finally ends a feud between brothers. He might be scribbling grocery lists and crossword answers. It doesn't matter to me. What matters is that he's doing it between two and four, when the rest of the city sleeps, when the traffic lights cycle through no one, when even the pigeons are unconscious on the concrete.

The diner has five stools at the counter. On nights when it's just him and me — because I'm always there too, that's the other part of the story — we form a kind of Parliament. The cook, whose name is Eddie, has never once acknowledged that we're there. He grunts when he brings orders. He says "mmhm" instead of "you're welcome." It's the purest form of human communication I've ever encountered.

Last Tuesday, something happened. The man with the journal stopped writing. He set the pen down, capped it, and stared at the eggs on his plate for what felt like a geological epoch. Then he looked at me — he never looks at me, we've never made eye contact, I'm certain of it — and he said: "Do you ever wonder if the version of you that the world knows is the one that's real, or if the real one only comes out at three in the morning?"

I said yes.

He said: "Good."

Then he picked up his pen and wrote for another hour.

I've been turning that over and over in my mind ever since, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand on a long walk, feeling its weight, its texture, the unexpected flat spot. Because he's right, isn't he? The version of me that answers emails and returns phone calls and nods through conversations about weather and mortgages — that's a performance. A skilled one, maybe, but a performance. The real me, the me that exists between two and four, that me doesn't perform. That me doesn't smooth things over. That me feels everything at full volume with no filter.

We have seven hours of authentic living, and they all happen after dark.

This thought has been changing me. Slowly, like rust changes iron — not all at once, but so gradually you don't notice until you realize you've become something entirely different from what you started. I've started saying what I actually think, not during the night hours, but during the day too. And I've discovered something terrible and liberating: people don't know what to do with it. A man at work asked if I liked the new policy and I said, "No, I think it's stupid and I think the person who wrote it knows it's stupid, and we all just pretend otherwise because pretending is easier than changing." There was silence. He blinked. He said, "Well, at least you're honest."

I don't think honesty and what I did are the same thing, but the line between them has always interested me.

Eddie the cook called me "kid" last week for the first time. I'm forty-three. He only did it when the other man with the journal wasn't in the booth. I think Eddie is afraid of him — not literally, not in a threat way, but in the way you're afraid of something you don't understand. The man with the journal is an unknown quantity to Eddie, to me, to anyone he interacts with. And the unknown, at three in the morning, over eggs and coffee, is the most powerful force in any room.

I've stopped trying to figure out what he writes in that journal. I've stopped trying to figure out why he's there. I've stopped trying to figure anything out, actually. The nightly ritual has taught me that some things are better left unresolved, that the mystery of another person is not a problem to be solved but a gift to be received, like someone silently handing you flowers through a window.

Tonight it's quiet. The city hums in its sleep. The neon sign of the diner flickers in a rhythm that's almost a heartbeat, almost a pulse, almost alive. The man with the journal is writing. Eddie is grunting behind the counter. I am here, being my truest self, in the only hours that belong to no one and everyone.

Tomorrow I'll be the performed version again. I'll nod and smile and say the right things in the right tone at the right time. But I'll know something the daytime version doesn't: that somewhere between two and four, I'll return to myself, and the self I find there will be more real than anything I said from nine to five.

The man with the journal just capped his pen. He's leaving.

Eddie says "mmhm" as he goes.

That's our language. That's all we need.
